headline: Analog Devices posts record revenue up 42%, but a flat first-quarter outlook sends the shares down 17%
takeaway: Fourth-quarter revenue rose 42% to $4.37 billion and full-year revenue 38% to a record $15.2 billion, with free cash flow of $5.5 billion. The guidance for a flat first quarter, landing in a day when chip stocks fell sharply, cut the shares 17.4% to $312.95.
results: Revenue grew 42% to $4.37 billion, led by data centre and industrial chips. Gross margin jumped to 69.3% from 63.1% (adjusted 74.5%), operating margin to 42.7% from 30.7%, and diluted earnings per share more than doubled to $3.40 (adjusted $4.06, up 80%).

For fiscal 2026, revenue rose 38% to $15.2 billion, a new high, and adjusted earnings per share 68% to $13.05. Operating cash flow was $6.2 billion and free cash flow $5.5 billion, 36% of revenue. ADI returned $5.4 billion to shareholders through $2.1 billion of dividends and $3.3 billion of buybacks.
mgmt: Chief executive Vincent Roche said AI investment is driving tremendous growth in its data centre and test equipment businesses, but that more than two-thirds of fiscal 2026 growth came from markets not centred on AI, such as industrial and automotive. Chief financial officer Richard Puccio said investment is going to research, capacity to secure customers’ supply, and steady capital returns.

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027 ADI forecast revenue of $4.4 billion, plus or minus $150 million, essentially flat with the fourth quarter, with adjusted operating margin of about 50.5% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.82, below the $4.06 just reported.
view: The year was outstanding: the analog chip cycle turned sharply upward, margins expanded by 12 percentage points and cash flow surged. The market’s reaction was about the next step. A flat revenue forecast and lower earnings per share for the first quarter tell investors the steep part of the recovery is behind it, and that came on a day when chip stocks were falling hard after Monday’s rally.

After the 17% drop, ADI trades at about 31 times trailing earnings and 17–18 times forward estimates. That is no longer expensive for the leading analog chipmaker, with margins near record highs and a broad base of industrial, automotive and data centre customers.

This turns on whether the cycle is peaking or pausing. Analog chips go through inventory cycles, and a flat quarter after such strong growth can be the start of a slowdown. But management’s point that most growth came from non-AI markets suggests the recovery is broad. I think the sell-off overstates the guidance, and the shares look reasonable for long-term holders, though the next two quarters will show which reading is right.
watch: Sequential revenue trends in industrial and automotive, gross margin, and whether the first-quarter guide proves conservative.
